sentences.text: Meridiocichla was an extinct genus of large thrushes that lived in Southern Europe during the Late Quaternary period. The only species, M. salotti, was the largest known thrush from Europe, roughly the size of a scaly thrush.
Despite its large size and island habitat, fossils show no evidence that Meridiocichla was flightless.

The only known fossils of Meridiocichla were found on the Mediterranean islands of Corsica and Crete. Fossils from Corsica include a premaxillary bone from Funtanedu Cave and humeri from Coscia Cave, while Crete yielded finds from Liko Cave.

The species was assigned to its own genus primarily because it had a large body size combined with a short, robust beak. The genus name Meridiocichla combines the Latin word for 'southern' and the Greek word for 'thrush'. The specific name commemorates paleontologist and archaeologist Michelle Salotti.
Meridiocichla was an omnivore, similar to other thrushes.
Researchers suggest its large size may have contributed to extinction by lowering population densities and making it vulnerable to sudden threats on islands.
Meridiocichla is classified within the family Turdidae.
Meridiocichla lived from the Late Pleistocene to the Holocene, between 0.129 and 0 million years ago.

It is unlikely the species was restricted only to Corsica and Crete, given unconfirmed remains from continental France, Italy, and Mallorca. Researchers suggest the Mediterranean islands may have served as wintering grounds rather than permanent habitats.
Meridiocichla was already rare during the Late Pleistocene and went extinct during the Late Pleistocene extinctions.

The exact phylogenetic relationships of Meridiocichla to other thrush species remain unclear. It is debated whether Meridiocichla belongs to the thrush family or is related to Old World flycatchers and whistling thrushes based on humerus comparisons.
